To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
deterministic public-key encryption can be made adaptively-secure, and that the price to be paid for this security level is a loss in efficiency.
(1) The security of the scheme of Bellare et al. is not guaranteed against plaintext distributions that depend on the public key.
we provide the first public-key encryption scheme that achieves security for adversarially chosen plaintext distributions that depend on the public key.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether there exists a deterministic public-key encryption scheme that is adaptively chosen-plaintext-secure against adversaries who can choose distributions depending on the public key of the scheme.
the following natural question: Can we extend the notion of security guarantees to include adversaries that have full knowledge of the public key?

the question: “Can we develop a notion of security for deterministic public-key encryption schemes that guarantees security against adversaries that can choose plaintext distributions adaptively and based on the public key?”
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we do not yet fully understand the exact power and limitations of deterministic public-key cryptography.
we currently do not know of a fully secure deterministic scheme.
we currently do not know whether deterministic public-key encryption is possible without further assumptions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we initiate the study of a new notion of security, called indistinguishability against adaptively chosen plaintext distributions (IND-ACPD-SEC), in which adversaries decide on plaintext distributions based on system parameters and possibly earlier plaintexts, and we put forward constructions with various guarantees.

the previous line of work on deterministic public-key encryption has been doing so at the expense of allowing adversaries to make use of trivially related plaintext attacks, where two distinct plaintexts are considered related if they are adaptively chosen based on each other in order to violate the security of the scheme.
we provide the first deterministic public-key encryption scheme providing a provable-security treatment in the presence of plaintext distributions that may depend adversarially on the public key.
The main takeaway from our work is that
determinism makes the achievement of provable security much more difficult in this setting.
, in contrast to the randomized case, this extension of the security requirement can be achieved without requiring strong computational assumptions.
deterministic public-key encryption can in fact be securely achieved in the face of adaptively chosen plaintext distributions (in the random-oracle model).
